title: Introducing peer support workers into an early intervention in psychosis service: a feasibility study
subtitle: Feasibility study with embedded interviews and progression criteria for a future trial
statement: An early intervention in psychosis team is introducing two part-time peer support workers for 12 months. It does not know whether young people will take up and stay in contact with peer support, whether peer workers can deliver the role as intended without burning out, or whether outcome questionnaires can be collected without extra appointments. A feasibility study with embedded interviews and explicit progression criteria would show whether a definitive trial is possible and worth doing.
whoAffected: About 210 young people aged 14 to 35 in their first three years after a first episode of psychosis, including under-18s; their families; the two peer support workers; and the clinical team.
whatHurts: Young people who drift away from the service in the first year lose treatment and support at the time it matters most; young men, cannabis users and people without stable housing are most affected. A peer role introduced without structure can harm the peer workers themselves.
currentPractice: Care coordination, medication and family work by the clinical team; no peer support workers; disengagement is followed up by the care coordinator.
whyNow: The innovation fund has paid for two peer support worker posts from January 2027, giving a single chance to evaluate their introduction.
constraints: Peer support worker posts funded for 12 months from January 2027; no other research funding. Evaluation uses routine data and short questionnaires only; no extra appointments for service users. Some participants are aged 14 to 17.
patientCenteredGoal: Young people with early psychosis stay connected with support that feels relevant to them, with peer workers who are themselves supported.
summary: Problem framed as a feasibility study of introducing peer support, with progression criteria for a later trial.
